content: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in Geneva has developed and published several standards related to water quality and the measurement of radioactive substances in water. These include: 1. ISO 11704 (2010): This standard outlines the methodology for measuring gross alpha and beta activity concentrations in non-saline water using liquid scintillation counting. 2. ISO 13160 (in preparation): This standard focuses on the measurement of strontium-90 and strontium-89 in water. 3. ISO 13161 (in preparation): This standard describes the measurement of polonium-210 activity concentration in water using alpha spectrometry. 4. ISO 13162 (in preparation): This standard provides guidelines for determining carbon-14 activity in water using liquid scintillation counting. 5. ISO 13163-1 (in preparation): This standard addresses the measurement of lead-210 activity concentration in water, specifically using liquid scintillation counting. 6. ISO 13164-1 (in preparation): This standard pertains to the measurement of radon-222 and its short-lived decay products in water, focusing on radon origins and measurement methods. 7. ISO 13164-2 (in preparation): This standard involves the direct measurement of radon-222 and its decay products in water using gamma spectrometry. 8. ISO 13164-3 (in preparation): This standard describes the indirect measurement of radon-222 and its decay products in water through degassing techniques. 9. ISO 13165-1 (in preparation): This standard focuses on the measurement of radium-226 activity concentration in water using liquid scintillation counting. Additionally, various studies and publications have contributed to the field of radiological analysis and water quality: Lariviere et al. (2009) discussed rapid and automated analytical technologies for radiological nuclear emergency preparedness in the context of nuclear chemistry research. NSF International (2005) provided a contaminant guide for water treatment. Pritchard and Gesell (1977) developed methods for rapid measurement of radon-222 concentrations in water using commercial liquid scintillation counters. Pritchard et al. (1991) explored liquid scintillation analysis of radon-222 in water with alpha/beta discrimination techniques. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) has also issued several guidelines and regulations: USEPA (1980) prescribed procedures for measuring radioactivity in drinking water. USEPA (1987) introduced two test procedures for radon in drinking water. USEPA (1999) and USEPA (2000) established national primary drinking water regulations for radionuclides, including radon-222. The World Health Organization (WHO) has contributed significantly to public health perspectives on water quality and radiological safety: WHO (2002) emphasized the importance of dialogue on risks from electromagnetic fields. WHO (2009) published a handbook on indoor radon from a public health perspective. These standards, studies, and guidelines collectively aim to ensure the safety and quality of drinking water by providing robust methodologies for detecting and measuring radioactive substances.
